title: Chicken Tinga
description: Shredded chicken simmered in a smoky chipotle-tomato sauce with soft onions, a Puebla home-kitchen staple used to fill tacos, tostadas and tortas across central Mexico.

ingredients.item: white onion, half quartered for poaching and half thinly sliced for the saute
garlic, divided (2 whole for poaching, 2 minced for the sauce)
canned chipotle peppers in adobo, finely chopped
ingredients.note: sold in small cans at Mexican/international aisles or online specialty groceries in Manila; use 1 tbsp for a milder household batch
regular dried oregano works fine
to taste; or a mild farmer's cheese if queso fresco isn't available

steps: Place the chicken in a pot with the water, the quartered half-onion and 2 whole garlic cloves; bring to a boil, then simmer 20 minutes until cooked through.
Lift out the chicken, reserve 1 cup of the poaching broth, and once cool enough to handle, shred the meat into bite-sized strips.
Blend the tomatoes, chipotles in adobo, remaining 2 garlic cloves, oregano, black pepper and the reserved broth until smooth.
Heat the oil in a wide skillet over medium-low heat and cook the sliced onion until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the blended sauce, raise the heat to medium and simmer uncovered 5-7 minutes until it darkens and thickens slightly.
Lower the heat, stir in the shredded chicken, cover and simmer 15-20 minutes until the sauce clings to the meat rather than pooling underneath.
Season with salt and serve warm over tostadas or folded into warm corn tortillas with crumbled queso fresco and avocado.
tips: Start with 1 tablespoon of chipotle for a mild family batch and pass extra chopped chipotle at the table for adults who want more heat.
Tinga tastes even better the next day; make it ahead and reheat gently with a splash of broth.
nutritionNote: Lean protein from chicken balanced by tomato; go easy on the oil and pair with a lime-dressed cabbage slaw or extra vegetables since the dish itself is light on fiber.

source.name: Mexican Food Journal (method verified against Mely Martinez's Chicken Tinga on Mexico in My Kitchen)

title: Carne Asada
description: Garlicky lime-marinated skirt steak grilled hot and fast, then sliced thin against the grain, the backbone of northern Mexican asada gatherings served with tortillas and salsa.

ingredients.note: ask the butcher for outer skirt steak; flank steak is an easy substitute
regular dried oregano works fine

ingredients.item: white onion, thickly sliced into rounds, for grilling

ingredients.note: sold frozen at Mexican/international grocers in Manila

ingredients.item: lime, cut into wedges, for serving

steps: Roast the unpeeled garlic cloves in a dry skillet over medium heat, turning often, until the skins are blotchy black and the cloves feel soft, about 10 minutes; cool, then peel.
Blend the roasted garlic with the lime juice, oil, oregano, salt and pepper into a loose marinade.
Pour half the marinade over the steak in a shallow dish, turning to coat, and let it sit at room temperature 20-30 minutes; reserve the other half.
Heat a charcoal or gas grill, or a heavy griddle pan, until very hot.
Grill the steak and onion rounds directly over the heat, about 3-4 minutes per side for the steak, until charred outside and still pink in the middle.
Rest the steak on a cutting board 5 minutes, then slice thinly against the grain.
Drizzle the sliced steak with the reserved marinade and serve with the grilled onions, warm corn tortillas and lime wedges.
tips: If marinating longer than 30 minutes, refrigerate the steak; lime juice starts to firm up the meat's surface if left too long at room temperature.
No grill? A cast-iron griddle screaming hot on the stovetop gets a very close result indoors.
nutritionNote: A good source of iron and protein; balance the fattier cut with extra grilled vegetables or a side salad, and keep tortilla portions modest for younger kids.

title: Cochinita Pibil
description: Pork shoulder marinated in tangy achiote and sour orange, wrapped in banana leaf and slow-roasted until it shreds with a fork, Yucatan's signature pit-style barbacoa adapted for a home oven.

ingredients.item: pork shoulder, cut into large chunks

ingredients.note: sold as achiote paste or recado rojo at Latin grocers; order online if unavailable in Manila, do not substitute plain paprika
or mix 3 parts regular orange juice to 1 part lime juice plus a splash of vinegar

ingredients.item: banana leaves, softened over a flame
ingredients.note: widely available fresh or frozen in Manila; or line the dish with parchment and foil if unavailable

ingredients.item: red onion, thinly sliced and pickled in lime juice

ingredients.note: serve on the side only, keep off the kids' plates entirely

steps: Blend the achiote paste, sour orange juice, lime juice, onion, garlic, salt and cumin into a smooth, brick-red marinade.
Coat the pork chunks thoroughly in the marinade, cover, and refrigerate at least 6 hours or overnight.
Soften the banana leaves briefly over an open flame or in a hot dry pan until pliable, then use them to line a deep baking dish, letting the edges hang over the sides.
Pour the marinated pork and all its liquid into the lined dish, then fold the banana leaf edges over the top to fully enclose the meat.
Cover tightly with foil and bake at 165C (325F) for about 3.5 hours, until the pork shreds easily with two forks.
Uncover, shred the pork directly in its juices, and stir in enough cooking liquid to keep it moist but not soupy.
Serve wrapped in warm corn tortillas, topped with pickled red onion, with sliced habanero on the side for anyone who wants extra heat.
tips: The pork must marinate at least 6 hours, overnight is better, for the achiote and citrus to fully penetrate; plan the day before.
No banana leaves is fine; the dish loses a little earthiness but the achiote and slow roasting still deliver the classic flavor.
nutritionNote: Pork shoulder is fattier than loin, so trim visible fat before marinating and serve with the pickled onion and extra shredded cabbage for acidity and fiber.

source.name: Isabel Eats (method cross-checked against Mely Martinez's Cochinita Pibil on Mexico in My Kitchen)

title: Veracruz-Style Fish
description: White fish fillets gently simmered in a Spanish-influenced tomato sauce with olives, capers and pickled jalapenos, Veracruz's coastal answer to Mediterranean flavors landing on Mexican shores.

ingredients.item: white fish fillets, about 150 g each
ingredients.note: red snapper (huachinango) is traditional; tilapia or cream dory are easy local substitutes
or use 1 can (400 g) whole peeled tomatoes, more reliable off-season
jalapenos en escabeche; or use pickled banana peppers if unavailable

ingredients.item: ground cinnamon or a pinch of nutmeg

steps: Season the fish fillets with lime juice and salt, then set aside while you make the sauce.
Heat the olive oil in a wide, deep skillet over medium heat and cook the onion until soft, about 4 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook 1 minute until fragrant, then stir in the chopped tomatoes, olives, capers, pickled jalapenos, bay leaf and cinnamon.
Simmer the sauce uncovered 10-12 minutes until it thickens and loses its raw-tomato smell.
Nestle the fish fillets into the sauce, spooning some sauce over the top, cover, and simmer gently 8-10 minutes until the fish flakes easily.
Taste and adjust salt, then remove the bay leaf.
Sprinkle with parsley and serve straight from the pan with white rice.
tips: Simmer the fish gently; a hard boil will break the fillets apart before they finish cooking.
Make the sauce up to a day ahead, it deepens in flavor overnight, and only poach the fish just before serving.
For the kids' plates, spoon sauce around the jalapeno slices rather than over them, or fish the slices out before serving.
nutritionNote: Lean white fish with tomatoes and olive oil is a heart-healthy combination; watch the sodium from olives and capers and skip added salt at the table.

title: Deviled Shrimp
description: Jumbo shrimp seared then bathed in a fiery guajillo and chile de arbol sauce, a beach-shack classic from the Pacific and Gulf coasts named for its glossy red heat.

ingredients.item: large shrimp, peeled and deveined, tails on

ingredients.note: dried guajillo chiles are sold at Mexican/specialty grocers online in Manila; buy extra, they keep well dried
this is where the real heat lives, omit entirely for the kids' batch and add back only for the adults' pot
or vegetable oil

ingredients.item: water, for soaking chiles and blending

ingredients.note: to taste

steps: Season the shrimp with salt and refrigerate while you make the sauce.
Toast the guajillo and arbol chiles briefly in a dry pan until fragrant, then cover with hot water and soak 15-20 minutes until soft; drain.
Blend the softened chiles with the tomatoes, garlic, cumin, onion and 1 cup fresh water until completely smooth.
For a kid-friendly batch, blend a second small portion of sauce using only the guajillo chiles, no arbol, and cook a portion of shrimp in that instead.
Melt the butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat and sear the shrimp about 1 minute per side, until just starting to turn pink; remove and set aside.
Pour the chile sauce into the same skillet, bring to a simmer, and cook 5 minutes until slightly thickened, scraping up the browned bits.
Return the shrimp to the skillet and toss to coat, cooking just 1-2 minutes more until opaque; do not overcook or the shrimp turn rubbery.
Scatter with cilantro and serve immediately with lime wedges, rice and warm tortillas.
tips: Buy the shrimp already peeled and deveined to keep this a genuine 30-minute weeknight dish.
Toasting the dried chiles 30 seconds per side before soaking deepens the flavor; watch closely, they burn fast.
kidNote: Blend a separate batch of sauce with guajillo only (no chile de arbol) for the kids' shrimp, and keep the arbol-spiked version in its own pan for the adults so everyone's plate matches their own heat tolerance.
nutritionNote: Shrimp is lean and high in protein; the sauce is chile-forward rather than creamy, so this pairs well with rice and a simple salad without adding much extra fat.

title: Green Enchiladas
description: Corn tortillas filled with shredded chicken, bathed in a bright tomatillo-serrano salsa and crema, then baked with melted cheese, central Mexico's classic Sunday-lunch enchilada.

ingredients.item: boneless, skinless chicken breast or thighs

ingredients.note: sold at some specialty grocers and online in Manila; or substitute drained canned tomatillos
use up to 2 for more heat, or deseed for milder
or sour cream thinned with a little milk

ingredients.item: queso fresco or Oaxaca cheese, crumbled or shredded

steps: Poach the chicken in a pot of water until cooked through, about 15-20 minutes; cool and shred into bite-sized pieces.
Simmer the tomatillos, serrano and garlic in the water for about 15 minutes until the tomatillos turn from bright to olive green and are soft.
Blend the cooked tomatillos, chile and garlic with the onion, 1 cup of the cooking water, crema and cilantro until smooth.
Warm a little oil in a skillet and quickly dip each tortilla a few seconds per side to soften without crisping.
Fill each tortilla with shredded chicken, roll it up, and lay seam-side down in a baking dish.
Pour the tomatillo-crema sauce evenly over the rolled enchiladas and scatter cheese on top.
Bake at 180C (350F) for 15-20 minutes until the cheese melts and the sauce bubbles at the edges.
Drizzle with extra crema, scatter sliced onion, and serve immediately while the tortillas are still tender.
tips: Dip, don't soak, the tortillas in warm oil; a few seconds keeps them pliable without turning greasy.
Assemble and refrigerate a few hours ahead, then bake just before serving so the tortillas don't go soggy.
nutritionNote: The crema and cheese add richness, so balance the plate with a simple side salad or extra shredded lettuce and tomato rather than more cheese.

source.name: The Kitchn (Mely Martinez's Enchiladas Verdes, from The Mexican Home Kitchen)

title: Cheese-Stuffed Poblano Chiles
description: Roasted poblano peppers stuffed with melting cheese, dipped in a fluffy egg batter and fried golden, then simmered briefly in a light tomato sauce, a Puebla classic that is mild, not fiery.

ingredients.note: poblano is a mild chile; large green bell pepper is a milder, less authentic stand-in if unavailable

ingredients.item: queso fresco or Oaxaca cheese, cut into strips

ingredients.note: dried guajillo and ancho chiles are available from Mexican specialty importers online in Manila

steps: Char the poblanos directly over a gas flame or under a hot broiler, turning until the skins blister black all over.
Seal the charred peppers in a plastic bag for 10 minutes to steam, then rub off the blackened skin under cool running water.
Slit each pepper lengthwise, leaving the stem intact, remove the seeds and veins, pat dry, and stuff generously with cheese strips.
For the sauce, boil the guajillo and ancho chiles 5 minutes to soften, then blend with the tomatoes, garlic, onion, broth and oregano until smooth; simmer 10 minutes and keep warm.
Beat the egg whites with the salt to soft peaks, then fold in the yolks to make a light batter.
Dust each stuffed pepper in flour, then dip fully in the egg batter to coat.
Fry in hot oil, turning once, until puffed and golden on all sides, about 3-4 minutes total; drain on paper towels.
Serve the fried chiles warm, napped with the tomato sauce.
tips: Keep a toothpick or two in the slit if the pepper wants to gape open; it holds the cheese in during frying.
Work with room-temperature cheese sticks so they melt through by the time the batter turns golden, without leaking out entirely.
nutritionNote: This is a fried, cheese-forward dish; balance the plate with the tomato sauce's vegetables and a side of rice or beans rather than more fried food.

source.name: My Latina Table (method cross-checked against Mely Martinez's Chile Relleno recipe on Mexico in My Kitchen)

title: Beans from the Pot
description: Dried pinto beans simmered low and slow with onion, garlic and epazote until creamy in their own broth, the everyday pot that feeds a Mexican family all week for very little money.

ingredients.item: dried pinto beans, sorted and rinsed
ingredients.note: bayo or flor de mayo beans also work; canned beans are not a substitute for this dish's texture
hard to find in Manila, order dried epazote online, or simply omit; the beans are still good without it
left whole and removed before serving, just for background flavor; omit entirely for a milder pot
lard gives the traditional flavor; oil is a fine substitute

steps: Spread the dried beans on a counter and pick out any small stones or shriveled beans, then rinse well in a colander.
Put the beans in a large pot with the water, onion, garlic, epazote and whole serrano; do not add salt yet.
Bring to a boil, reduce to a low simmer, cover partially, and cook 1.5 to 2 hours, topping up with hot water as needed to keep the beans submerged.
Check for tenderness after about an hour; the beans are ready when they mash easily against the side of the pot with a spoon.
Once tender, stir in the salt and lard, and simmer another 15-20 minutes so the broth thickens slightly.
Remove the serrano and epazote, then serve the beans in bowls with their broth, or mash and fry a portion into refried beans another day.
tips: Never salt dried beans before they're tender; it toughens the skins and they'll never fully soften.
This pot freezes well; portion it out for a ready side or taco filling for weeks.
nutritionNote: An excellent source of plant protein and fiber; this is the backbone of a balanced Mexican plate alongside rice, vegetables and a small portion of meat.

title: Mexican Noodle Soup
description: Toasted vermicelli coils simmered in a light tomato broth until just tender, the everyday soup Mexican kids grow up on, made with pantry staples in about twenty minutes.

ingredients.note: coiled vermicelli sold as fideo or fideos cortados; broken thin spaghetti or vermicelli noodles work as a substitute
about 400 g

steps: Blend the canned tomatoes with their juice, garlic, oregano, salt and cumin until completely smooth.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat, add the dry fideo noodles, and stir constantly 3-4 minutes until they turn from pale to deep golden brown.
Carefully pour in the blended tomato mixture, it will spatter, and stir to coat the toasted noodles.
Add the broth, bring to a boil, then reduce to a simmer, cover, and cook 5-7 minutes until the noodles are tender but not mushy.
Taste and adjust the salt.
Ladle into bowls and top with cilantro, queso fresco, avocado and a squeeze of lime.
tips: Toasting the noodles until deep golden, not just tan, is what gives this soup its nutty flavor; don't rush this step.
The noodles keep absorbing broth as they sit, so serve immediately or thin with extra broth when reheating.
nutritionNote: A light, easy-to-digest soup that's gentle on kids' stomachs; add extra broth or a side of beans to make it a more complete meal.

title: Mexican Red Rice
description: Rice toasted in oil until golden, then simmered in a blended tomato, garlic and onion sauce until every grain turns out fluffy and separate, the standard side for nearly every Mexican meal.

ingredients.note: optional, for a heartier side
left whole for aroma only, removed before serving; omit for a completely mild pot

steps: Rinse the rice under cold water until it runs mostly clear, then drain well.
Blend the tomatoes, onion and garlic with half a cup of the broth until completely smooth; set aside.
Heat the oil in a saucepan over medium heat and toast the rice, stirring often, until it turns opaque and pale golden, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the blended tomato mixture, it will sizzle, stirring to coat every grain, and cook 2 minutes to cook off the raw tomato taste.
Add the remaining broth, carrots and peas if using, the whole serrano, cilantro sprig and salt; stir once.
Bring to a boil, reduce to the lowest heat, cover tightly, and cook without lifting the lid for 15 minutes.
Remove from heat and let it rest, covered, 10 minutes, then fluff with a fork before serving.
tips: Stir the rice only once it hits a boil; constant stirring after that releases starch and makes it gummy instead of fluffy.
Resist lifting the lid while it cooks; the trapped steam is doing the work.
nutritionNote: A simple carbohydrate side; pair with beans and a protein like tinga or carne asada to round out the plate with fiber and protein.

source.name: Mexico in My Kitchen (Mely Martinez's Arroz Rojo method, cross-checked against RecipeTin Eats)

title: Mushroom Quesadillas
description: Corn tortillas griddled with melted Oaxaca cheese and mushrooms sauteed with epazote and chile, a Mexico City street-stall staple that also makes a fast, meatless weeknight dinner.

ingredients.note: wild mushrooms are traditional in central Mexico; button or cremini are the easiest reliable substitute
deseed for a milder filling, or omit entirely
hard to find in Manila, order dried epazote online, or substitute a little chopped cilantro plus a pinch of dried oregano
mozzarella is the closest easy substitute

steps: Heat the oil in a skillet over medium heat and cook the onion until translucent, about 3 minutes.
Add the mushrooms, chile and garlic, stir well, and cook uncovered, stirring occasionally, until the mushrooms release their liquid and it mostly evaporates, 6-8 minutes.
Stir in the epazote and salt in the last minute of cooking, then remove from heat.
Warm the corn tortillas on a dry griddle or comal until pliable, about 20 seconds per side.
Place a tortilla on the griddle, scatter cheese over half, top with a spoonful of the mushroom filling, and fold the tortilla over.
Press gently and cook 1-2 minutes per side until the tortilla is lightly toasted and the cheese has melted through.
Serve immediately with salsa on the side.
tips: Let the mushrooms fully release and cook off their own liquid before folding the quesadilla, or the tortilla will turn soggy.
Corn tortillas tear more easily than flour; warm them first so they fold without cracking.
nutritionNote: A meatless, fiber-rich option; the cheese provides protein and calcium, but keep portions moderate to avoid excess saturated fat if serving often.

source.name: Mexico in My Kitchen (sauteed mushroom filling), assembly per La Cocina de Leslie's Quesadillas de Hongos

title: Red Pozole
description: Pork and hominy simmered in a deep guajillo-ancho broth and finished at the table with cabbage, radish and lime, the celebration soup for birthdays and Mexican Independence Day.

ingredients.item: pork spare ribs or baby back ribs
ingredients.note: or use all pork shoulder if ribs aren't available
cacahuazintle hominy sold canned or frozen at Latin/specialty grocers online in Manila; canned white corn kernels are a last-resort substitute though the texture differs
order dried guajillo and ancho chiles from a Mexican/Latin specialty grocer online if a local market doesn't carry them; they keep for months dried
table-only garnish, this is where the real heat is added; keep it off the kids' bowls entirely and let each adult spoon in their own

steps: Combine the pork shoulder, ribs, quartered onion and whole garlic cloves in a large pot with the water; bring to a boil, skim the foam, then reduce to a gentle simmer 2 to 2.5 hours until the meat is fork-tender.
Lift out the meat, discard the bones and any large fat, shred or chunk the meat, and return it to the strained broth.
Meanwhile, soak the guajillo and ancho chiles in a bowl of hot water 20-25 minutes until soft and pliable.
Drain the chiles and blend them with the sauce garlic, oregano and a cup of the broth until completely smooth.
Heat the oil in a skillet, pour in the chile puree, and simmer 10 minutes, stirring often as it will splatter, until it deepens in color.
Strain the chile sauce into the pot of broth and meat to keep the pozole silky, add the drained hominy, and simmer 20-30 minutes until the hominy is tender.
Season with salt, keeping the pot itself mild; do not add chile piquin to the pot.
Ladle into deep bowls and let everyone garnish their own portion with cabbage, onion, radish and lime, adding crushed piquin or hot salsa only to the bowls that want it.
tips: This is a weekend project; the broth alone needs 2 to 2.5 hours, so start it in the morning for an evening meal.
Straining the chile puree into the broth removes the tough chile skins and keeps the pozole smooth rather than gritty.
kidNote: Keep the pot's chile base to guajillo and ancho only, it's warm, not fiery, and put the crushed chile piquin and any hot salsa out as table garnishes so each person, including the kids, spoons in their own heat.
nutritionNote: A hearty, protein-rich stew with fiber from the hominy; load up the table-side cabbage and radish to round it into a fuller vegetable serving.

source.name: Cooks Without Borders (Mely Martinez's Pozole Rojo)
